analysis.one_liner: Slashes power plant sulfur dioxide, smog-forming, and mercury emissions to curb acid rain.
analysis.headline: The Acid Rain Control Act never left committee: after referral to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its energy subcommittee in early 2003, it received no hearing, no vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2005.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have cut the national cap on sulfur dioxide from power plants roughly in half (from 8.9 million tons to 3 million tons a year after 2011), set a hard national limit on nitrogen oxides, and required the EPA to write rules controlling mercury from power plants by the end of 2004, with no trading of mercury pollution credits. It would have kept emissions trading for sulfur and nitrogen, required reductions in both eastern and western regions to prevent local pollution hot spots, and ordered EPA to report on whether the cuts were enough to protect sensitive waters and mountains from acid damage.
analysis.who_benefits: People living downwind of coal- and oil-fired power plants, especially in the Northeast and mid-Atlantic, would get less acid rain damaging lakes, forests, and buildings, and less smog and mercury contaminating fish and water supplies.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Downwind residents, anglers, and sensitive ecosystems

how_it_helps.text: Cut the annual sulfur dioxide cap for utility plants from 8.90 million tons to 4.45 million tons for 2008–2011 and to 3 million tons thereafter, roughly a two-thirds reduction, which is the pollutant that causes acid rain [S3].
Set national nitrogen oxide limits of 2.10 million tons for 2008–2011 and 1.70 million tons from 2012 on, with a $6,000-per-ton penalty for excess emissions, targeting smog and acid deposition [S3].

Required the EPA to issue mercury controls for electric utilities and industrial sources by December 15, 2004, and barred the transfer of mercury allowances, meaning each plant would have to cut its own mercury rather than buy its way out [S3].

Required EPA regulations to prevent localized pollution hot spots and to achieve significant reductions in both the Eastern and Western regions, addressing the problem that emissions trading can concentrate pollution near particular communities [S3].

Directed EPA to identify environmental indicators, including acid neutralizing capacity, for the Adirondacks, mid-Appalachians, Rockies, Blue Ridge, Great Lakes, Lake Champlain, Long Island Sound, and Chesapeake Bay, and to tighten rules further if the cuts proved insufficient to protect those ecosystems [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Coal- and oil-fired electric utilities and their industrial customers would bear the cost of installing scrubbers and other controls, a cost that would likely be passed at least partly to electricity ratepayers, with the heaviest burden on coal-dependent regions and coal mining employment.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs for power plants would be substantial and would likely flow into higher electricity prices, falling hardest on coal-dependent states and communities whose jobs depend on coal mining and burning [S3].

The bill kept market-oriented mechanisms such as emissions trading for sulfur dioxide and nitrogen oxides, which can let some plants keep polluting by buying allowances elsewhere, though it tried to guard against this by requiring prevention of localized adverse effects [S3].

The bill itself acknowledged uncertainty about how much reduction was enough: it required EPA to report by 2011 on whether the mandated cuts were sufficient to protect sensitive ecosystems, and to promulgate further regulations only if they were not [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public health and ecosystem gains from sharply lower sulfur, nitrogen, and mercury emissions are broad and long-lasting, and the bill's flexibility mechanisms (trading for sulfur and nitrogen, strict no-trading for mercury) were designed to lower compliance costs. The real cost is concentrated: higher electricity prices and job losses in coal regions, which is exactly why the bill faced utility and coal-state resistance. On balance the design is defensible, though the delayed trigger for further ecosystem protections (not before 2011) means the most sensitive waters could keep degrading for years.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and sent to its energy subcommittee three weeks later, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Republican Rep. John Sweeney of New York introduced the Acid Rain Control Act on January 7, 2003, joined by Rep. John McHugh of New York [S3].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, the committee with jurisdiction over the Clean Air Act [S1].
On February 3, 2003, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality, where it remained for the rest of the 108th Congress [S5].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a subcommittee vote, a committee markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005 [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Coal- and oil-fired electric utilities came out ahead: without the new caps, they avoided roughly a two-thirds cut in sulfur dioxide, new nitrogen oxide limits, and mandatory mercury controls, along with the compliance costs those would have required. People living near acid-sensitive lakes, forests, and downwind of power plants gained nothing from the bill's death except continued exposure to the status quo emissions.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Coal-fired power plants that avoided new controls

for.name: Rep. John E. Sweeney
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Acid Rain Control Act mandating deep cuts in power plant sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and mercury.

for.name: Rep. John M. McHugh

sides.party_line_note: The bill's sponsorship was bipartisan, with 7 of its 11 cosponsors Republican and 4 Democratic, but its fate was decided by the Republican-run Energy and Commerce Committee, which never brought it up; the record contains no roll-call votes.

industries.note: The bill would have cut their allowed sulfur dioxide emissions by roughly two-thirds, imposed national nitrogen oxide limits with a $6,000-per-ton penalty, and required mercury controls that could not be traded away. Their interest in blocking it ran directly against downwind residents' interest in cleaner air and water [S3].
Deep cuts in sulfur dioxide emissions reduce demand for high-sulfur coal, threatening mining jobs in producing regions. The industry's interest ran against the public's interest in reduced acid rain.
Mandatory emissions cuts would have created demand for flue-gas desulfurization and other control technology, and those reductions also serve the public's health interests.
